findings.description: The RDS instance sets publicly_accessible = true, so the MySQL endpoint is reachable from the public internet. Combined with ingress from the whole VPC CIDR and an admin username, this materially expands the attack surface for brute-force and exploitation of the database.

storage_encrypted = false leaves the database's EBS storage, automated snapshots, and read replicas unencrypted, so anyone with access to the underlying storage or a snapshot copy can read the data in plaintext.

The master credential is the static, non-managed username "admin" with the password taken from var.password and stored in Terraform state; the lifecycle ignore_changes on password means it can never be rotated by Terraform. Static admin credentials in state create a persistent, long-lived privileged secret.

The EC2 user_data script embeds the database password (var.password) and endpoint into /var/www/inc/dbinfo.inc. user_data is not encrypted by default and is readable via the instance metadata service (IMDS) and by anyone with ec2:DescribeInstanceAttribute, exposing the DB credential.

The policy grants s3:*, ec2:*, and rds:* on Resource "*", giving the application instance full control over all S3 data, all EC2 instances (including creating/terminating and IAM instance profiles), and all RDS databases in the account. Compromise of the instance yields broad account-wide privilege escalation.

The ingress rule opens MySQL port 3306 to the entire VPC CIDR block rather than to the application security group specifically. Any resource in the VPC — including any compromised or unauthorized instance — can reach the database.

The database security group allows all outbound traffic (protocol -1, 0.0.0.0/0). A database should not initiate arbitrary outbound connections; this facilitates data exfiltration and lateral movement if the DB host is compromised.

The parameter group does not set require_secure_transport (or equivalent SSL enforcement), so clients may connect to MySQL in plaintext, allowing the DB credentials and query data to be intercepted on the network.
The output exposes the application server's public DNS name, which reveals the internet-facing entry point of the application to anyone who can read state or plan output.
